items.title_en: Korean etiquette — and why it works this way
items.summary_en: Age and respect shape a lot of daily life in Korea. This comes from Confucian tradition. Know the why, and the small rules make sense.

points_en: Confucian ideas have been part of daily life in Korea since the Three Kingdoms period, and shaped society under the Joseon dynasty (1392–1910).
Confucianism gives people a place by age and social rank. That is why age matters here, and why Korean has polite forms of speech.
Respect for elders and ancestral rites are still part of Korean family life. Jongmyo Shrine in Seoul is where the Joseon royal family held these rites.

do_en: Greet people with a short bow — a small nod is enough.
Give and receive things with both hands, especially with older people.
Take your shoes off at the door of homes, temples and guesthouses.
dont_en: Point at people with your finger.
points_en: Tipping is not expected. Some places accept it, some will refuse it.

do_en: Wait until the oldest person starts eating.
Rice on the left, soup on the right. Spoon on the left, chopsticks on the right.
dont_en: Stand chopsticks or a spoon up in your rice — this is done in rites for the dead.
Lift your rice or soup bowl to your mouth.

do_en: Hold the glass or bottle with both hands when you pour for, or receive from, someone older.
Turn your head slightly away from the older person when you drink.
End sentences with -yo (for example, gamsahaeyo) when talking to older people or strangers. It sounds polite.
Let people finish talking before you answer.

items.title_en: Gyeongbokgung: the story before you go
items.title_ko: 경복궁, 가기 전에 알면 좋은 이야기
items.summary_en: Seoul's main palace was built in 1395, burned, rebuilt, torn down again, and is still being restored. Here's what you're looking at — and when to go.

timeline.text: Built by King Taejo, three years after the Joseon dynasty began. The name means the new dynasty will have good fortune and prosper.
Destroyed during the Japanese invasion. It stayed in ruins for about 270 years.
Rebuilt by King Gojong (work began in 1865).
Under Japanese rule, most buildings were torn down. In 1926 a colonial government building went up on the palace grounds.
The colonial building was removed. Restoration had begun in the 1990s.
Gwanghwamun Gate area restored — gates and royal quarters have been rebuilt step by step.

points_en: Much of what you see is rebuilt, following old records — that is part of the story, not a copy.
Okhoru, in the Geoncheonggung area at the back, is where Empress Myeongseong was killed in 1895.
Royal Guard Changing Ceremony at 10:00 and 14:00, at Heungnyemun and Gwanghwamun gates.
Gwanghwamun gate guard ceremony at 11:00 and 13:00.
It recreates the Joseon royal guard, a system set up in 1469, with costumes and weapons based on old records.
It may be cancelled in rain, and times can change — check the official site on the day.
Entry is free if you wear hanbok (traditional Korean clothes).
Free English tours run most days at 11:00, 13:30 and 15:30 — see the palace page for details.
